chief_complaint: burning upper abdominal pain 2 hours after meals relieved by food
hpi_details: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning upper abdominal pain 2 hours after meals relieved by food. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks drinking strong coffee on an empty stomach produces excessive acid that is irritating and burning her stomach lining.
concerns: She is worried that the gnawing burning sensation is an early sign of stomach cancer, which her father died of in his early fifties.
expectations: She hopes to leave with a prescription for a strong acid reducer and a referral for an endoscopy to check her stomach lining.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Peptic Ulcer Disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Peptic Ulcer Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes testing for and treating H. pylori infection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: burning upper abdominal pain 2 hours after meals relieved by food

Key HPI features: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning upper abdominal pain 2 hours after meals relieved by food. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Peptic Ulcer Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Peptic Ulcer Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: haematemesis or melena, sudden severe abdominal pain with rigidity, unintentional weight loss, early satiety, or persistent vomiting.
management_principles: Perform H. pylori urea breath test, initiate triple therapy eradication
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of burning upper abdominal pain 2 hours after meals relieved by food. HPI: H. pylori infection, NSAID use.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Peptic Ulcer Disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Peptic Ulcer Disease.
reference_soap.plan: Assess for alarm features and NSAID use. Test for H. pylori with an appropriate noninvasive test, holding acid suppression when required for accuracy. Treat confirmed infection using a locally appropriate regimen, commonly bismuth quadruple therapy when susceptibility is unknown, and confirm eradication after treatment.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Peptic Ulcer Disease
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Peptic Ulcer Disease
Implement evidence-based management plan: Perform H. pylori urea breath test, initiate triple therapy eradication

teaching.one_liner: An ulcer in the stomach or duodenum, usually from H. pylori infection or NSAID use, causes burning epigastric pain a couple of hours after meals that eating can actually relieve.
red_flags: Haematemesis or melena — suggests active ulcer bleeding
Sudden severe abdominal pain with rigidity — suggests perforation
Unintentional weight loss, early satiety, or persistent vomiting — raises concern for gastric malignancy or outlet obstruction

must_ask.say: Does the pain come on a couple of hours after eating, and does eating actually make it better?
Do you take ibuprofen or any other painkillers regularly?
Have you ever been tested or treated for H. pylori infection?
Have you had any black stools, vomited blood, or unplanned weight loss?
Do you smoke, or drink alcohol regularly?
Does the pain ever wake you up at night?

history.answer: I have been having this burning pain in the middle of my upper stomach, especially when my stomach is empty about two hours after eating.
It feels like a gnawing, burning sensation right in the pit of my stomach.
The burning is centered in my upper abdomen right below the ribs, and it does not travel to my back or chest.
It started about three weeks ago and has been gradually getting more intense and frequent over the past few days.
The pain typically comes on about two hours after a meal when my stomach empties, and eating a snack or drinking milk eases it right away.
Yes, I frequently wake up around two or three in the morning with a burning hunger pain in my stomach.
No, I do not have acid or sour fluid backing up into my throat, nor a burning feeling behind my breastbone, and lying down does not worsen it.
No, I can eat a normal-sized meal without feeling full too early.
No, swallowing is completely smooth and painless with no feeling of food getting stuck.
My appetite has been fairly normal, and my weight has not changed at all.
No, I have never vomited blood or coffee-ground material, and my bowel movements are normal brown without any black or sticky stool.
I sometimes feel slightly queasy when the burning gets bad, but I have not thrown up.
I have been feeling somewhat tired and run-down lately, but I have not had any dizziness or lightheaded spells.
No, I have not had severe pain attacks under my right ribs after eating greasy or fatty foods.
No, walking fast or climbing stairs does not trigger or worsen the discomfort in my chest or stomach.
I took over-the-counter ibuprofen a few times last month for headaches, but I do not take aspirin or pain relievers on a daily basis.
I drink one cup of coffee every morning and try to avoid late-night snacks, though I occasionally have spicy food.
I had a routine screening endoscopy about three years ago that showed mild gastritis, but I have never been tested or treated for Helicobacter pylori.
No, no one in my immediate family has had stomach cancer or any other gastrointestinal cancer.
I thought maybe drinking strong coffee on an empty stomach produced too much acid and is eating away at my stomach lining.
My dad passed away from stomach cancer in his early fifties, so I'm deeply worried this constant burning could be cancer too.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or liver problems.
I have never undergone any surgical operations and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, herbal remedies, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I only drink an occasional glass of beer or wine once or twice a month at social dinners.
I work full-time as an administrative office worker and live at home with my husband.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my monthly cycles have been regular.
My husband had a vasectomy several years ago, so there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Patient is alert, well-nourished, and in mild discomfort from epigastric aching, without acute distress.
Blood pressure is 120/76 mmHg, heart rate is 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are white without icterus.
No lymphadenopathy is palpated in the cervical chains or supraclavicular fossae, with no left supraclavicular enlargement.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without surgical scars, visible pulsations, or distension.
Normoactive bowel sounds are heard across all four quadrants with no abdominal bruits.
Mild focal tenderness is elicited upon deep palpation in the epigastric region, without guarding or palpable masses.
No rebound tenderness is present in any abdominal quadrant.
Murphy sign is negative with no tenderness or arrest of inspiration on right upper quadrant palpation.
Digital rectal examination demonstrates normal sphincter tone, no palpable mass, and brown stool on the glove with negative occult blood.
